question: What is the main reason doctors order a skin snip test?

options.A: Detecting dermal microfilariae of Onchocerca volvulus
options.C: Measuring deep dermal thickness for burn assessment
options.D: Identifying fungal elements in superficial tinea

explanation: You got this! A skin snip is specifically used to catch tiny parasite larvae (microfilariae) hiding in the skin layers. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T13#GNS213_U5_T13_h1)

question: Which patient symptom from an endemic region makes you suspect they might need a skin snip test?

options.A: Chronic intense itching and skin changes
options.B: Severe joint pain and high spiking fevers
options.C: Painful fluid-filled blisters on the lips

explanation: Spot on! Onchocerciasis (river blindness) is famous for causing stubborn, severe itching, bumps, and changes in skin texture where the parasite lives. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T13#GNS213_U5_T13_h1)

question: Which piece of patient history is most critical for a nurse to check before a skin snip?

options.A: A history of bleeding disorders or anticoagulant use
options.B: Previous surgery for appendicitis years ago
options.C: Mild seasonal allergies to pollen and dust
options.D: A childhood diagnosis of uncomplicated asthma

explanation: Safety first! Because a skin snip involves a tiny cut, we always check if the patient bleeds easily or takes blood thinners. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T13#GNS213_U5_T13_h2)

question: A patient scheduled for a skin snip is very anxious about pain. What is your best first response?

options.A: Cancel the procedure immediately without consulting the doctor
options.B: Administer general anesthesia to keep the patient completely asleep
options.C: Explain the procedure steps and reassure them about local anesthetic use
options.D: Tell the patient that the procedure is entirely painless and quick

explanation: Great nursing judgement! Walking patients through the steps and letting them know local numbing will be used calms their nerves. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T13#GNS213_U5_T13_h2)

question: Why is local anesthetic WITHOUT epinephrine typically chosen for a skin snip?

options.B: Epinephrine instantly destroys the surgical scalpel blade
options.C: Local anesthetics cannot be mixed with epinephrine under any rule
options.D: Vasoconstriction can interfere with parasite emergence from the tissue

explanation: Exactly. We want blood vessels to stay open so the tiny live parasites can easily crawl out of the skin sample into our liquid solution. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T13#GNS213_U5_T13_h3)

question: What is the main goal of placing the harvested skin sample into normal saline or water?

options.A: To sterilize the sample from any surface bacterial contamination
options.B: To encourage the microfilariae to emerge out into the fluid
options.C: To dissolve the tissue completely so only DNA remains
options.D: To preserve the tissue for permanent paraffin embedding

explanation: Spot on! The liquid tricks the live microfilariae into crawling right out of the skin snippet so we can spot them under the microscope. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T13#GNS213_U5_T13_h3)

question: How deep should the blade go when performing a standard skin snip?

options.A: Superficially into the dermis without deep cutting
options.B: Strictly through the dead outer stratum corneum layer
options.C: Deep into the subcutaneous fat layer for fat cells
options.D: Through the entire muscle layer down to the bone

explanation: You got it! Since the little parasites hang out in the upper skin layers (dermis), we only need a very shallow snip. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T13#GNS213_U5_T13_h4)

question: What does the clinician usually do right before cutting the skin with the scalpel?

options.A: Elevating a small cone of skin using a sterile needle
options.B: Applying deep pressure to stop all local circulation
options.C: Stretching the skin tightly in four opposite directions
options.D: Massaging the area vigorously to numb it faster

explanation: Correct! Lifting a tiny tent of skin helps the clinician snip just the right top layer safely without cutting too deep. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T13#GNS213_U5_T13_h4)

question: What causes the microfilariae to leave the skin sample and enter the liquid?

options.A: Active migration of the living parasites into the fluid
options.B: Electrical current passed directly through the glass vial
options.C: Chemical digestion of skin cells by strong laboratory acids
options.D: Mechanical centrifugation at high speeds in the machine

explanation: Well done! The living parasites actively wiggle and crawl out of the skin tissue into the surrounding water or saline. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T13#GNS213_U5_T13_h5)

question: Why is proper labeling crucial when taking skin snips from different body parts of the same patient?

options.A: To speed up the microscope staining process safely
options.B: To calculate the exact financial cost of laboratory processing
options.C: To determine how much local anesthetic was injected
options.D: To track which anatomical site yielded the parasites

explanation: Spot on! Parasite concentration can differ across body sites, so knowing the exact spot helps doctors measure how heavy the infection is. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T13#GNS213_U5_T13_h5)

question: What is your immediate nursing action right after the skin snip is taken?

options.A: Scrubbing the bleeding wound vigorously with soap
options.B: Applying direct pressure to the site until bleeding stops
options.C: Suturing the tiny wound closed with heavy nylon thread
options.D: Placing an ice pack directly on the open raw tissue

explanation: Correct! Simple direct pressure stops any minor bleeding at the tiny biopsy site before putting a bandage on. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T13#GNS213_U5_T13_h6)

question: A patient calls two days post-procedure reporting mild redness and tenderness. What should you advise?

options.A: Scrape the bandage off and wash the wound with harsh bleach
options.B: Come in immediately for emergency surgical debridement
options.C: Stop all prescribed medications and start strong intravenous antibiotics
options.D: Reassure the patient that mild tenderness is normal, but watch for worsening signs

explanation: You nailed it! A little bit of soreness during healing is totally normal, but we always teach patients what red flags (like pus or spreading redness) to watch out for. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T13#GNS213_U5_T13_h6)
